name: Sound Detectives
subtitle: Aural skills and the elements of music
blurb: Ten weeks of listening. You build a toolkit for describing what you hear, use it on jazz, film music and Australian music, and learn to write about music with evidence.
outcomes: uses listening skills to analyse music in relation to style and context
analyses how the musical concepts are manipulated and combined in a range of repertoire

assessment.name: AT3 Listening Examination
assessment.detail: Four short-answer excerpts and one extended response. 20 marks, worth 25%.

weeks.title: The Elements Toolkit
weeks.intro: Welcome to our listening unit. This week we meet the six elements of music and learn to describe what we hear in clear, musical language.

lessons.title: Active listening and the elements of music
lessons.intention: I can name the elements of music and use them to describe what I hear.
criteria: I can identify at least three elements in a short excerpt.
I can use the right word for each element.

blocks.brief: An engaging contemporary track to listen to first (teacher choice). Students just listen and jot what they notice.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Listen to the track and jot down anything you hear.
Meet the six elements of music: duration, pitch, texture, performing media & timbre, dynamics & expression, structure.
Add each term to your listening glossary.
Listen again and tag what you hear to an element.

blocks.text: Make a list of every element you can hear in the track, with one word describing how it is used.
Name three elements you heard today.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck to introduce the six elements.

lessons.title: Duration and pitch (listen and play)
lessons.intention: I can identify duration and pitch features by ear.
criteria: I can describe the tempo, metre and rhythm of an excerpt.
I can describe a melody’s shape (contour) and range.

blocks.text: How music moves through time: is it fast or slow, are the notes short or long, does it have a steady beat or does it feel off-kilter?
How high or low the notes are, and what the melody does: does it climb, fall, stay put?

blocks.brief: A short rhythmic example (clear beat and metre) and a short melodic example (clear melody) , one of each.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap: duration = beat, tempo, metre, rhythm. Pitch = melody, contour, range.
Write the definitions of duration and pitch in your books.
Clap or play the rhythm patterns as a class.
Play or sing the short melodies and describe their shape.
Listen and identify these features by ear.

blocks.text: Notate or describe a 4-bar rhythm you hear, then describe the contour of a short melody (rising, falling, wave).
Was the melody’s range wide or narrow? How do you know?

lessons.title: Writing about music 1
lessons.intention: I can write a clear sentence about how an element is used.
criteria: My sentence names the element.
It says how the element is used and its effect, with evidence.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the response sentence: element + how it is used + effect + evidence.
Build a class response to a short excerpt together.
Write one paragraph on your own.
Swap with a partner and check against the sentence frame.

blocks.text: Write one paragraph about a short excerpt using the sentence frame for at least two elements.
Underline the ‘effect’ part of your best sentence.

teacher: Model the sentence on the board: element + how it is used + effect + musical evidence. Build one together before students write.

weeks.title: Texture, Timbre and Comparing
weeks.intro: This week we listen across styles to explore texture and timbre, and learn how to compare two works using the elements of music.

lessons.title: Texture across styles (listen and build)
lessons.intention: I can identify and describe texture in different styles.
criteria: I can name the texture type (monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic).
I can explain how the layers combine.

blocks.text: The way layers of sound are combined in a piece of music.

blocks.brief: Suggestions: Gregorian chant (search ‘Gregorian chant Kyrie’), or unaccompanied solo voice/instrument.

blocks.text: A single melodic line with no accompaniment.

blocks.brief: Suggestions: a simple pop or hymn arrangement (e.g. a band playing melody over strummed/block chords), or a piano/vocal ballad.

blocks.text: A melody with chordal accompaniment.

blocks.brief: Suggestions: a Bach fugue (e.g. ‘Little Fugue in G minor’), a round/canon (e.g. ‘Frère Jacques’ sung in canon), or a jazz combo with independent improvised lines.

blocks.text: Two or more independent melodic lines combined.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Read the texture definition and each texture type.
Listen to the excerpt after each definition and check it matches.
In groups, build a texture by adding one layer at a time.
Describe how the texture changed as layers were added.

blocks.text: For each excerpt, name the texture type and explain how the layers combine to create it.
Which excerpt had the thickest texture, and why?

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (texture section) for the diagrams.

lessons.title: Performing media and timbre
lessons.intention: I can identify performing media and describe timbre.
criteria: I can name the instruments or voices I hear.
I can describe their tone colour using musical words.

blocks.text: What's making the sound, and what it actually sounds like — an instrument's ‘personality’.

blocks.brief: World: a raga on solo sitar — a distinctive, sustained plucked-string timbre.
Jazz: Louis Armstrong's trumpet and gravelly vocal timbre, instantly recognisable.
Film: the Star Wars Main Title, full orchestral timbre.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap: performing media = the sound sources; timbre = their tone colour.
Listen and build a class ‘timbre word bank’ (bright, warm, harsh, mellow, etc.).
Play an instrument ID quiz with short clips.
Match a timbre word to each instrument you hear.

blocks.text: For each clip, name the instruments or voices and give one word for their tone colour.
Pick one instrument and describe its timbre in a full sentence.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (timbre section).

lessons.title: Comparing 'Valerie'
lessons.intention: I can compare two versions of the same song using performing media and timbre.
criteria: I can name the voices and instruments I hear in each version.
I can describe the tone colour of each one using musical words.
I can write one similarity and one difference, and back each up with musical evidence.

blocks.text: The voices and instruments used to perform a piece of music — in other words, what is making the sound.

The quality of a sound that makes one voice or instrument sound different from another, even when they play exactly the same note. A trumpet and a flute playing the same pitch do not sound the same, and timbre is the word for that difference.

blocks.brief: Version A: The Zutons, 2006 — the original.
Version B: Mark Ronson featuring Amy Winehouse, 2007 — same melody, words and chords, completely different performing media and timbre.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Copy both definitions into your book, and the timbre word bank.
Listen once through to each version without writing anything: who is singing, what carries the hook, what holds the rhythm, what sits on top.
Listen again and rule up a table in your book: the voice, the instrument that leads, the rhythm section, anything else you can hear, and three tone-colour words for each version.
Every comparison point needs three parts: name it, give the evidence you heard, and explain the effect.

blocks.text: Write one similarity and one difference between the two versions, each backed with musical evidence and its effect. Performing media and timbre are marked together as one 2-mark question in the listening exam — naming the instruments alone only gets you one mark, you need the tone-colour description too.
Which version's tone colour suits the song better, and why? Name at least one voice or instrument in your answer.

weeks.title: Dynamics, Structure and Exam Writing
weeks.intro: This week we finish the toolkit with dynamics, expression and structure, and start writing full responses to the exam question.

lessons.title: Dynamics and expression
lessons.intention: I can identify dynamics and expression and explain their effect.
criteria: I can describe how the volume changes.
I can explain how a change in dynamics changes the mood.

blocks.text: How loud or soft the music is, and the little performance tricks (sliding, plucking, shaking a note) that add feeling.

blocks.brief: A film music cue with clear dynamic changes (quiet build to a loud climax).

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap: dynamics = volume; expression = the detail that gives a style its feel (articulation, accents).
Listen to the film cue and follow a listening map of the dynamics.
Mark where the music gets louder or softer and what happens to the mood.
Add expression words (legato, staccato, accent) to your glossary.

blocks.text: On a listening map, track the dynamics of the cue and write one sentence on how a change in dynamics changed the mood.
Name one moment where dynamics created tension.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (dynamics & expression section).

lessons.title: Structure
lessons.intention: I can identify the structure of a work by ear.
criteria: I can label the sections of a work.
I can describe how the sections differ.

blocks.text: How the piece is put together — the order of its sections, like the shape of a story.

blocks.brief: A pop song with a clear verse-chorus structure.

blocks.text: The pop-song structure: verses tell the story, the chorus is the hook that repeats.

blocks.brief: A 12-bar blues.

blocks.text: A repeating 12-bar chord pattern, often with an AAB lyric pattern — the backbone of blues and early rock 'n' roll.

blocks.brief: A classical work in ternary form or theme and variation.

blocks.text: Ternary (ABA): a section, a contrasting middle, then a return to the start. Theme and variation: one melody, dressed up differently each time it repeats.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap forms: verse-chorus, 12-bar blues, ternary (ABA), theme and variation.
Listen and map the sections of each excerpt.
Discuss what tells you a new section has started (a change in an element).
Compare how the three structures are organised.

blocks.text: Map the structure of one excerpt by labelling its sections and noting what changes between them.
What element signalled a new section most clearly?

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (structure section).

lessons.title: Writing about music 3: the exam question
lessons.intention: I can write an extended response on how elements create interest.
criteria: My response covers several elements.
Each point has evidence and an effect.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Meet the exam-style question.
Watch the teacher model a full response across several elements.
Plan your response using a paragraph planner.
Write a full timed response and self-assess against the criteria.

blocks.text: Write a full response to a short excerpt answering: how are the elements of music used to create interest?
Which element gave you the strongest point to write about?

teacher: Introduce the AT3 exam question: ‘How are the elements of music used to create interest?’ Model a full response, thinking aloud.

weeks.title: Wide Listening and Exam Preparation
weeks.intro: This week we listen widely across genres and rehearse the exam: full responses, feedback and strategies, ready for AT3 next week.

lessons.title: Wide listening carousel
lessons.intention: I can quickly identify style and elements across genres.
criteria: I can identify the style of each excerpt.
I can name two key elements for each.

blocks.brief: World: Gamelan gong kebyar, 'Kapi Raja' — a distinctive percussive, metallic ensemble.
Classical: Vivaldi, Spring (The Four Seasons) — energetic Baroque strings.
Film: Hedwig's Theme — John Williams, instantly recognisable orchestral timbre.
Jazz: Take Five — the Dave Brubeck Quartet, an odd 5/4 metre.
Contemporary: As It Was — Harry Styles.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Rotate through the five listening stations.
At each station, identify the style and two key elements.
Log your answers as you go.
Compare answers as a class at the end.

blocks.text: Complete your listening log: style + two elements + one effect for each of the five excerpts.
Which style was easiest to identify, and what gave it away?

lessons.title: Extended response practice and feedback
lessons.intention: I can write to the standard of the AT3 task.
criteria: I can apply feedback to improve a response.
My response uses evidence and correct terminology.

blocks.brief: Studied-style: What a Wonderful World — Louis Armstrong, already analysed for timbre.
Unseen: Bohemian Rhapsody — Queen, for timed extended-response practice.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Write a full timed response to the studied excerpt.
Swap with a partner and give feedback against the criteria.
Read the teacher feedback and the common misconceptions.
Write a second response to the unseen excerpt.

blocks.text: Improve your first response using the feedback, then attempt the unseen excerpt under time.
Name one thing you will do differently in the exam.

lessons.title: Exam strategies and review
lessons.intention: I can use effective strategies in a listening exam.
criteria: I can annotate an excerpt as I listen.
I can plan a response under time pressure.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the strategies: annotate while listening, use the replays, manage your time, use your terminology bank.
Quick-fire revision of the six elements.
Practise annotating a short excerpt in real time.
Ask any final questions before the exam.

blocks.brief: Grieg, 'In the Hall of the Mountain King' (Sydney Symphony Orchestra / Ashkenazy) — unseen, and short enough to annotate start to finish. Tempo, dynamics and texture all build together, so it gives real-time practice catching several elements changing at once.

blocks.text: Annotate a short excerpt as it plays, then plan (not write) a full response in two minutes.
Write down your personal exam plan in one sentence.

teacher: Hand out the strategy checklist and terminology bank. Do a final quick-fire revision of all six elements.

weeks.title: AT3 Exam and Feedback
weeks.intro: This week you sit the AT3 Listening Examination, then return to practical playing and review your responses to set goals.

lessons.title: AT3 Listening Examination
lessons.intention: I can analyse how the elements of music are manipulated and combined.
criteria: I complete the exam with accurate, evidenced responses.
I use correct musical terminology.

blocks.text: (No exit ticket , exam lesson.)

teacher: Set up exam conditions and audio playback. Apply access provisions (reader, scribe, extra time, separate supervision) as per plans.

lessons.title: Practical recovery lesson
lessons.intention: I can contribute to a group performance with awareness.
criteria: I can keep my part in time.
I can listen and adjust to the ensemble.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Return to instruments for some low-stakes ensemble playing.
Choose a song to play together as a class.
Re-engage your performing and creating skills after the exam.

blocks.text: Play a class ensemble piece, focusing on timing and listening to others.
One thing your group did well today.

lessons.title: Exam feedback and reflection
lessons.intention: I can evaluate my own listening response and set a goal.
criteria: I can name one strength and one improvement.
I understand what a strong response looks like.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Read your marked response and the feedback.
Compare your answer to the exemplar answers.
Identify one strength and one next step.
Set a personal listening goal for the rest of the term.

blocks.text: Re-draft one weak paragraph from your exam to a higher standard using the exemplar.
Write your listening goal for the rest of Term 3.

teacher: Return marked responses. Model exemplar answers band by band so students see the standard.

weeks.title: Jazz
weeks.intro: This week we listen to jazz, play a 12-bar blues and improvise, then analyse how jazz uses the elements of music to create interest.

lessons.title: Jazz listening
lessons.intention: I can identify the features and context of jazz.
criteria: I can name three features of jazz.
I can hear where improvisation happens.

blocks.brief: Vocal/standard: Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong, 'Summertime' — the classic jazz-standard vocal duo sound.
Big band: Glenn Miller, 'In the Mood' — the archetypal swing-era big band riff and ensemble sound.
Small-combo bebop: Charlie Parker, 'Ornithology' (1946) — fast bebop with an audible improvised alto solo.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the context: where and when jazz developed.
Meet the key features: swing, improvisation, blue notes, instrumentation.
Listen to the three excerpts and spot these features.
Identify the instruments and where the improvised solos are.

blocks.text: For each excerpt, tick the jazz features you hear and mark where a solo is improvised.
How can you tell a section is improvised rather than written?

teacher: Use the ‘Jazz’ deck for context and key features.

lessons.title: Jazz practical: 12-bar blues
lessons.intention: I can perform and improvise within a 12-bar blues.
criteria: I can keep my place in the 12-bar form.
I can play a short improvised idea.

blocks.brief: 12-bar blues backing track in A major, 100 bpm — a comfortable tempo for the class to play along with and improvise over.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the 12-bar blues chord pattern.
Take a role: chords, bass, rhythm or melody.
Play through the form as a class with the backing track.
Try a short improvised solo using the blues scale.

blocks.text: Perform the 12-bar blues as an ensemble; everyone attempts at least a two-note improvised idea.
Did you keep your place in the form? What helped?

lessons.title: Analysing a jazz recording
lessons.intention: I can analyse a jazz work using the elements of music.
criteria: I can explain how improvisation and structure create interest.
I use evidence and terminology.

blocks.brief: Miles Davis, 'So What' — modal jazz with clear structure (intro/head/solos/head) and distinct instrumental timbres, ideal for written analysis.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Listen to the recording twice.
Plan your response using element prompts.
Write about how improvisation, structure and timbre create interest.
Swap for peer feedback against the criteria.

blocks.text: Write a response: how does this jazz recording use the elements of music to create interest?
Which element was most important in this recording?

weeks.title: Film Music
weeks.intro: This week we explore how film music creates mood and tells stories, create a short cue, and analyse a film composer’s choices.

lessons.title: Film music listening
lessons.intention: I can identify how film music supports narrative.
criteria: I can link a musical feature to an emotion or scene.
I can use the term leitmotif correctly.

blocks.brief: John Williams, 'Star Wars' Main Title — heroic, adventurous mood.
John Williams, 'Jaws' Theme — suspense and dread from a simple two-note idea.
Michael Giacchino, 'Married Life' (from 'Up') — poignant, emotional storytelling without dialogue.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Meet the techniques: leitmotif, underscore, mickey-mousing.
Listen to the cues and match musical features to on-screen meaning.
Connect back to Term 1 program music and your Term 2 soundtrack task.
Discuss how the elements signal emotion.

blocks.text: For each cue, link one musical feature to the emotion or action it supports.
What does a leitmotif do in a film?

teacher: Use the ‘Film Music’ deck for techniques and examples.

lessons.title: Film music practical / compose
lessons.intention: I can use an element of music to create a mood for a scene.
criteria: I can create a short cue.
I can explain the element I used and its effect.

blocks.brief: 'Sintel' (Blender Foundation, Creative Commons) — mute the sound and cue a 20-30 second scene for students to score.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Choose a clip or mood to score.
Pick one element to focus on (e.g. tempo, timbre or dynamics).
Create a short cue using flat.io, a DAW or instruments.
Share and explain the effect you aimed for.

blocks.text: Create a 20-30 second cue that uses one element to set a clear mood for the scene.
Which element did you use, and what mood did it create?

lessons.title: Analysing a film cue
lessons.intention: I can analyse film music using the elements of music.
criteria: I can explain how two elements support the narrative.
I use evidence and terminology.

blocks.brief: Hans Zimmer, 'Cornfield Chase' (Interstellar) — building dynamics and layered texture, rich material for a two-element analysis.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Listen to the cue twice.
Plan using element prompts.
Write about how the composer manipulates two elements to support the scene.
Check your evidence and terminology.

blocks.text: Write a response on how this film cue uses the elements of music to support the story.
Name the two elements you wrote about.

weeks.title: Music of Australia and First Nations Music
weeks.intro: This week we listen to and analyse music of Australia, including music of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, with respect for context and protocols.

lessons.title: Music of Australia and First Nations music
lessons.intention: I can describe Australian music and its context respectfully.
criteria: I can link features of the music to its cultural context.
I use respectful, accurate language.

blocks.brief: Gurrumul, 'Wiyathul' — Yolŋu language, official video, gentle traditional-influenced example.
Baker Boy ft. Yirrmal, 'Marryuna' — contemporary First Nations hip-hop, official video, blends language and beats.
King Stingray, 'Get Me Out' — contemporary Yolŋu-language surf-rock, official video, broadens the styles on offer.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Discuss what we mean by music of Australia, including First Nations music.
Listen with respect and attention to context (cultural, historical, social).
Note the instruments, language and stories where shared by the artists.
Connect features of the music to its context.

blocks.text: For one work, describe two musical features and explain how they connect to the music’s context.
One thing you learned about the context of an Australian work.

teacher: Use the ‘Music of Australia & First Nations Music’ deck (includes protocols).

Follow respectful protocols and ICIP awareness. Where possible, seek local community consultation and use artist-approved recordings. Avoid sacred or restricted material. Centre First Nations voices and artists.

lessons.title: Australian music analysis
lessons.intention: I can analyse an Australian work using elements and context.
criteria: I can explain how the music reflects its context.
I use evidence and terminology.

blocks.brief: Yothu Yindi, 'Treaty' (Radio Mix, official video) — blends traditional Yolŋu music with rock; rich land-rights context for a context-linked analysis.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Listen to the work twice.
Plan using both element prompts and context prompts.
Write about how the elements are used and how the music reflects its context.
Share and discuss using musical terminology.

blocks.text: Write a response linking the elements of music to the context of an Australian work.
How did context shape the way you heard this work?

lessons.title: Practical and response: Australian styles
lessons.intention: I can perform a feature of an Australian style and describe it.
criteria: I can play the feature accurately.
I can name the element it demonstrates.

blocks.brief: Men at Work, 'Down Under' (official video) — an instantly recognisable riff/groove the class can play, tying the element directly to an iconic Australian sound.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn a short riff or groove from an Australian popular style.
Take a role and perform it as a group.
Discuss which elements make the style recognisable.
Write a brief reflection linking the playing to the elements.

blocks.text: Perform the riff or groove, then name the element it best demonstrates and why.
Which element makes this style instantly recognisable?

weeks.title: Comparative and Critical Listening
weeks.intro: This week we compare how styles use the elements differently, evaluate interpretive choices, and start thinking about the Term 4 Depth Study.

lessons.title: Comparative listening across styles
lessons.intention: I can compare how an element is used across styles.
criteria: I can explain similarities and differences.
I support each point with evidence.

blocks.brief: Orchestra: Holst, 'Jupiter' (The Planets) — full, densely layered orchestral texture.
EDM: Avicii, 'Levels' — texture built and dropped through electronic layering.
A cappella: Pentatonix, 'Hallelujah' — texture created entirely from layered voices.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Choose one element to focus on (e.g. texture).
Listen to the three excerpts.
Build a class comparison, then write your own.
Use comparison language and evidence.

blocks.text: Compare how your chosen element is used across the three excerpts, with one similarity and two differences.
Which style used the element most surprisingly?

lessons.title: Critical listening: evaluating choices
lessons.intention: I can evaluate interpretive choices in performance.
criteria: I can compare two versions of a work.
I can justify a preference with musical evidence.

blocks.brief: Vivaldi, 'Spring' (traditional recording, already analysed in Lesson 10).
Max Richter, 'Recomposed: Vivaldi's Four Seasons — Spring 1' — a radically different interpretive take on the same material.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Listen to both versions of the work.
Note the differences in tempo, dynamics, expression and timbre.
Decide which you find more effective and why.
Justify your judgement with musical evidence.

blocks.text: Write a short evaluation: which version is more effective, and what musical evidence supports your view?
Name one interpretive choice that changed the feel of the work.

lessons.title: Student-choice listening and Depth Study spark
lessons.intention: I can analyse music I choose and identify a personal area of interest.
criteria: I can present a short analysis of my chosen track.
I can name an area I might pursue in the Depth Study.

blocks.brief: Students may bring their own track (cleared as school-appropriate) to analyse.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Choose a track you care about.
Analyse it using the six elements.
Share a short analysis with a partner or the class.
Note a style, artist or skill you might explore in the Depth Study.

blocks.text: Present a 1-minute analysis of your chosen track, then write the area you might pursue in Term 4.
What is your possible Depth Study interest?

teacher: Introduce the Term 4 Depth Study and show the idea-bank menu. Students start thinking about a focus area.

weeks.title: Synthesis and Depth Study Launch
weeks.intro: This week we present our analyses, launch the Term 4 Depth Study, and finish with an approved proposal ready to develop.

lessons.title: Synthesis presentation
lessons.intention: I can present a clear analysis of a work.
criteria: I can explain how several elements create interest.
My presentation is clear and well organised.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: In a small group, choose a work to analyse.
Plan a short multimodal presentation (audio + key points).
Present to the class.
Give one strength and one question to each group.

blocks.text: Present your group analysis of how several elements create interest in your chosen work.
One thing another group did well in their analysis.

teacher: Frame this as a model for how a listening Depth Study can be presented (including viva voce).

lessons.title: Depth Study launch and idea generation
lessons.intention: I can generate realistic Depth Study ideas that match my interests and skills.
criteria: I have shortlisted two possible projects.
I know the focus area of each.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn what a Depth Study is and how it works.
Explore the idea bank: performing, composing, listening and combinations.
Brainstorm ideas that match your interests and skills.
Shortlist two possible projects.

blocks.text: Write down two possible Depth Study projects and the focus area of each.
Which of your two ideas excites you most, and why?

teacher: Optional: show the Depth Study idea bank from the Term 4 unit on the board.
Walk through the Depth Study: purpose, the 8-10 hours, and that students choose their focus. Explore a modelled work sample.

lessons.title: Depth Study proposal (milestone) and term celebration
lessons.intention: I can write a clear, realistic plan for my Depth Study.
criteria: My proposal states what I will make.
It states the outcomes I will show and how I will judge success.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Complete the Depth Study proposal: focus, goal, product, outcomes, steps, resources, success criteria.
Get teacher feedback on your plan.
Adjust your proposal so it is realistic for the time.
Celebrate the term with a wide-listening quiz.

blocks.text: Finish and submit your Depth Study proposal for approval.
What is the first step you will take in Term 4?

teacher: Review each proposal and give feedback so students start Term 4 ready to develop. Run a wide-listening quiz to celebrate the term.
